a: A homeowners association (HOA) is an organization that manages a planned community (subdivision, condo building, townhome complex) and enforces its rules. When you buy a home in an HOA community, membership is mandatory — it comes with the deed. What it does: (1) Enforces CC&Rs (covenants, conditions, and restrictions) — rules about paint colors, lawns, fences, parking, pets, holiday decorations, and more. (2) Maintains common areas — landscaping, clubhouse, pool, roads, and in condos, the building exterior and roof. (3) Collects dues (monthly or annual) and special assessments (one-time fees for big repairs) and manages a reserve fund. The trade-off: HOAs keep the neighborhood uniform and well-maintained (which supports property values), but they cost money and restrict what you can do with your own home — and poorly-run HOAs can be bureaucratic or intrusive. Before buying in an HOA: read the CC&Rs and the budget/reserve study, check the dues and whether they've risen steeply, attend a board meeting if you can, and ask how much is in the reserve fund (low reserves often mean big special assessments coming). If an HOA fines you unfairly, you have appeal rights spelled out in your state's laws and the governing documents — but the practical rule is: know the rules before you buy, because once you sign, you've agreed to them.
